prompt: What does Kanban ask a team to change on the first day?

choices.text: Its calendar
choices.why: Kanban has no fixed iterations.

choices.text: Its roles
choices.why: Kanban adds no roles; it starts with the ones you have.

choices.text: Its tools, moving everything to a board product
choices.why: A paper board works; the tool is not the change.

choices.text: Only to make its work visible
choices.why: Right. Change comes afterwards, one experiment at a time.

prompt: Which practice does the lesson call the one that makes the rest work?
hint: A board without it is a picture.

choices.text: Limiting work in progress
choices.why: Right. Without limits, the board shows the queues and nothing stops them growing.

choices.text: Holding a daily meeting in front of the board
choices.why: Kanban prescribes no meetings.

choices.text: Making the exit policies explicit on every column
choices.why: Useful, and it depends on limits to matter.

choices.text: Visualising the work
choices.why: Necessary, but a board with no limits is only a picture.

prompt: Match each origin to what it contributed.

pairs.right: Cards that request more parts: a pull system
The Kanban Method and its six practices
The Kanban Guide and its four measures

prompt: Developing and Review are both at their limits. A developer has just finished a task. What does the board say they should do?

choices.text: Pull a new card from Ready into Developing
choices.why: Developing is at its limit, so pulling breaks the rule.

choices.text: Push it into Review anyway
choices.why: Review is full; pushing would exceed its limit.

choices.text: Help clear the Review column
choices.why: Right. The free capacity is downstream; finishing beats starting.

choices.text: Raise Review's limit
choices.why: Raising a limit the first time it bites removes what it was for.

prompt: What does splitting Developing into doing and done make visible?

choices.text: How many points each card is worth
choices.why: Kanban boards need no points.

choices.text: Who is working on each card
choices.why: That is what an avatar on the card shows, not the split.

choices.text: Which cards are blocked by another team
choices.why: A blocker marker shows that; the split shows waiting for capacity.

choices.text: Finished work that is queuing
choices.why: Right. Without the split, waiting cards look like cards being worked on.

prompt: A stakeholder says an item 'took five weeks', and the team says its cycle time was five days. Can both be right?

choices.text: No: the two are the same
choices.why: They start their clocks at different points.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the team works in Sprints
choices.why: The distinction has nothing to do with Sprints.

choices.text: Yes, two different clocks
choices.why: Right. Lead time counts from the request, cycle time from the commitment point; the item waited about a month before anybody started it.

choices.text: No: one of them is measuring wrongly
choices.why: Both are legitimate measures of different intervals.

prompt: When a card leaves Ready, it crosses the ___ point, and its clock starts.
hint: The team promises to finish it.

prompt: A team finishes 5 items a week whatever it does, and keeps 10 items in progress. By Little's law, about how many weeks does an item take on average?
hint: Cycle time is work in progress divided by throughput.

prompt: Of an item's seven days of cycle time, two were work and five were waiting. What does a limit on Review attack?

choices.text: The time spent in testing
choices.why: The limit is on Review; testing would need its own.

choices.text: The two days of development work
choices.why: The limit does not make anybody type faster.

choices.text: The number of people on the team
choices.why: Limits are on cards, not people.

choices.text: The queue before it
choices.why: Right. A short queue is crossed faster; the work itself is untouched.

prompt: A manager wants items to finish sooner and asks the team to start more work in parallel. With throughput unchanged, what happens by Little's law?
hint: Hold throughput fixed and raise work in progress.

choices.text: Nothing changes
choices.why: Throughput is fixed; cycle time is what moves.

choices.text: Throughput doubles to match the work started
choices.why: The question holds throughput unchanged.

choices.text: Every item takes longer on average
choices.why: Right. Cycle time is work in progress divided by throughput.

choices.text: Items finish sooner because more are open
choices.why: More open items with the same throughput means longer waits.

prompt: A column's limit is never reached in three months. What does the lesson say about it?

choices.text: It should be removed, since Kanban needs none
choices.why: Limits are what make Kanban Kanban.

choices.text: It should be raised to leave room for growth
choices.why: Raising it limits even less.

choices.text: It is set perfectly
choices.why: A limit that never binds forces no conversation.

choices.text: It is not limiting anything and should come down
choices.why: Right. A limit matters on the day it is hit.

prompt: Why does the course recommend LibreOffice Calc over the other two paths?

choices.text: The course cannot be followed in Google Sheets
choices.why: Either of the other paths gives the same numbers.

choices.text: It is the only one with a percentile function
choices.why: All three have it.

choices.text: It runs the course's lessons in the browser
choices.why: It is installed and runs on your computer, not in a browser.

choices.text: Free, offline, and the spreadsheet that computed the course's values
choices.why: Right. Its numbers match the lessons exactly.

prompt: An item started and finished on 4 March. With the Agenda team's convention, what is its cycle time?

choices.text: It cannot be measured until the next day
choices.why: The dates are known; the formula gives it at once.

choices.text: Two days, start plus finish
choices.why: Start and finish are the same day, counted once.

choices.text: One day
choices.why: Right. The +1 counts both the start and the finish day.

choices.text: Zero days
choices.why: That is the result without the +1, which the team does not use.

prompt: Why does the lesson ask you to write dates as 2026-03-02?
hint: Think of spreadsheets in other languages.

choices.text: It sorts better on paper
choices.why: Sorting is a side benefit, not the reason given.

choices.text: It is the only format LibreOffice accepts
choices.why: It accepts others, depending on the locale.

choices.text: Every locale reads it as a date
choices.why: Right. Day and month order differs by locale; year-month-day does not.

choices.text: It makes the cycle time come out one day longer
choices.why: The format does not change the arithmetic.

prompt: Match each symptom to its likely cause.
hint: One of them shows no error at all.

pairs.right: A function name from another language

pairs.left: Every cycle time a day short

right_distractors: A column that is too narrow

prompt: One date in a column of twenty is text. What happens to =MEDIAN over the whole column, by the course's run?

choices.text: It returns #VALUE! too
choices.why: Right. One error in the range makes the summary an error.

choices.text: It returns #NAME?
choices.why: #NAME? is for an unknown function.

choices.text: It returns zero
choices.why: Nothing in the run returned zero.

choices.text: It ignores the bad row and returns the median of 19
choices.why: That would hide the problem; the spreadsheet does not.

prompt: Which mistake does the lesson call the most dangerous, and why?
hint: Think about what the screen shows.

choices.text: A date stored as text, because #VALUE! spreads
choices.why: It spreads, but it is visible on the screen.

choices.text: A function name in Portuguese, because it cannot be fixed
choices.why: Retyping the name fixes it.

choices.text: Leaving off the +1: every number is wrong and nothing says so
choices.why: Right. An error message gets noticed; a quiet off-by-one does not.

choices.text: Using a semicolon, because English spreadsheets reject it
choices.why: LibreOffice accepts it in either language.

prompt: What is the median cycle time of the Agenda team's twenty items, in days?
hint: The middle of the sorted list.

prompt: What does PERCENTILE.INC return for the 85th percentile of those cycle times? Give one decimal place.
hint: It is the line in the figure.

prompt: Why is the mean cycle time (7.75 days) above the median (7)?

choices.text: The median is rounded
choices.why: The median of 20 values here is exactly 7.

choices.text: A few slow items pull it up
choices.why: Right. Cycle times are skewed: nothing is under a day, a few are very long.

choices.text: The median ignores the items that finished in March
choices.why: All twenty finished in March and all are counted.

choices.text: The mean counts weekends and the median does not
choices.why: Both use the same Days column.

prompt: A stakeholder asks how long the next item will take. Which answer does the lesson recommend?
hint: A statement about the team's own history.

choices.text: It depends on the estimate for that item
choices.why: No estimate is needed; the dates already answer.

choices.text: Between 2 and 19 days, the full range
choices.why: Honest, but the range is too wide to plan around.

choices.text: Exactly 7.75 days, the mean
choices.why: A single number hides the spread, and the mean is pulled by outliers.

choices.text: Most items finish within about twelve days
choices.why: Right. That is the 85th percentile, a service level expectation.

prompt: How many items did the Agenda team finish on average per week over the four weeks?
A platform team receives unpredictable requests from other teams that must be answered within days. Which method fits better, by the lesson?

choices.text: Kanban, with continuous flow
choices.why: Right. Sprints would hold urgent requests or be broken every few days.

choices.text: Neither; it needs a sequential plan
choices.why: Nothing about the work is knowable in advance.

choices.text: Scrum, because it has a Product Owner
choices.why: A Product Owner does not make arrivals predictable.

choices.text: Scrum, with one-week Sprints
choices.why: Even a week is long for a request that needs a day.

prompt: Which of these does Scrum prescribe and Kanban does not? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An explicit limit per column
choices.why: That is Kanban's, not Scrum's.

choices.text: Measuring cycle time
choices.why: Kanban names it as a core measure.

choices.text: Fixed-length iterations
choices.why: Yes: Sprints of a month or less.

choices.text: Named accountabilities such as the Product Owner
choices.why: Yes: Kanban starts with the roles you have.

prompt: Put these in the order a card meets them on the Agenda team's board.
hint: The clock starts at the second.
trap: The commitment point is crossed when the card leaves Ready, before any development.

prompt: A team's board has no limits, and its cycle times keep growing while everybody is busy. Which change does the lesson predict will shorten them without anybody working faster?

choices.text: Setting WIP limits
choices.why: Right. Less work in progress at the same throughput means shorter cycle times.

choices.text: Estimating every card in points
choices.why: Estimates measure nothing about the queue.

choices.text: Adding a column for each person
choices.why: More columns change the picture, not the queue.

choices.text: Switching to Sprints
choices.why: Sprints limit work only by what fits; the question is about the board.
